HIV Drug Formulations and Usage: Dolutegravir (DTG) 10 mg Dispersible Tablets: These are used as first-line or second-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) for infants and children aged 4 weeks or older, weighing between 3 and less than 20 kg. They are available in packs of 90 tablets. Abacavir (ABC) + Lamivudine (3TC) 120 mg/60 mg Dispersible Tablets: These are preferred for first-line or second-line ART in children weighing 3–25 kg. They are available in packs of 30 or 60 tablets. Zidovudine (AZT) Oral Solution 50 mg/5 mL: This is used for postnatal prophylaxis and neonatal treatment during the first four weeks of life. It is supplied in 240 mL bottles. Nevirapine (NVP) Oral Solution 50 mg/5 mL: This is used exclusively for postnatal prophylaxis and neonatal treatment. It is available in 100 mL bottles. Lopinavir/Ritonavir (LPV/r) 100 mg/25 mg Heat-Stable Tablets: These are an alternative for first-line or second-line ART in children weighing 10 kg or more who can swallow tablets whole. They are supplied in packs of 60 tablets. LPV/r Oral Granules 40 mg/10 mg: These are used as an alternative for first-line or second-line ART in infants and children weighing 10 kg or less or those unable to swallow whole tablets. They are available in packs of 120 sachets. AZT + 3TC 60 mg/30 mg Dispersible Tablets: These are used for second-line ART in children weighing 3–25 kg. They are supplied in packs of 60 tablets. 2. Preferred Formulations for Children: For children weighing 20 kg or more, the preferred formulation is DTG 50 mg film-coated tablets. For those weighing 30 kg or more, a co-formulated tablet containing DTG 50 mg, Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF) 300 mg, and 3TC 300 mg (known as TLD) is recommended to reduce pill burden, simplify supply chains, and lower program costs. 3. Limited-Use ARV Formulations: NVP 50 mg Dispersible Tablets: Used only for postnatal prophylaxis when the oral solution is unavailable. 3TC Oral Solution 50 mg/5 mL: Used exclusively for neonatal treatment during the first four weeks of life. Raltegravir (RAL) Granules for Suspension 100 mg: Used for neonatal treatment during the first four weeks of life. LPV/r Oral Pellets 40 mg/10 mg: Used in specific cases where DTG 10 mg tablets or LPV/r oral granules are unavailable or clinically indicated. Darunavir (DRV) Tablets (75 mg, 150 mg): Used in third-line ART regimens for children aged three years and older. Ritonavir (RTV) 25 mg Tablets: Used for super-boosting LPV/r during tuberculosis (TB) treatment or when administering DRV. 4. Implementation of Pediatric ARV Formulations: National programs are encouraged to limit procurement to formulations listed in the Optimal Pediatric Formulary to simplify supply chains and stabilize global ARV drug supplies for children. 5. Service Delivery Considerations: Age-appropriate fixed-dose combinations are preferred for children. Dispersible tablets or granules are ideal as they can be converted into liquid form for easier administration. Oral liquid formulations should be avoided when solid oral dosage forms are available. Neonates typically require oral liquid formulations, but transitioning to solid forms is recommended as soon as possible. 6. Introduction of New Products: Introducing new medicinal products in HIV programs is complex and requires careful planning. Factors such as patent restrictions, product registration, demand forecasting, and procurement budgets must be considered. Collaboration with global buyers and pooled procurement mechanisms can help address challenges related to low-demand products. 7. Laboratory and Diagnostic Services: Strengthening laboratory and diagnostic services is critical for implementing HIV guidelines. This includes expanding access to diagnostics like infant diagnosis, CD4, and viral load testing, as well as ensuring quality assurance and proper placement of testing platforms. Point-of-care testing and electronic communication systems, such as SMS/GSM/GPRS printers, can reduce turnaround times for test results, especially in rural settings. 8. Specimen Referral Systems: Integration of referral systems across diseases can improve efficiency. 9. Electronic Communication for Test Results: Electronic systems, such as SMS/GPRS printers, have been shown to reduce turnaround times for early infant HIV diagnosis results. These systems can also be applied to other laboratory tests to improve efficiency and equity in rural areas. 10. Quality Assurance in Diagnostics: A robust quality assurance system is essential for ensuring accurate and reliable diagnostic services. This includes planning, implementing, and monitoring quality assurance processes, as well as training and certifying healthcare workers. 11. Strategic Planning for Diagnostics: National laboratory strategies should focus on optimizing diagnostic networks, harmonizing testing platforms, and ensuring adequate resources for infrastructure, human resources, and quality assurance mechanisms. 12. Recommendations for Procurement and Supply Management: Procurement managers should consider factors such as product shelf life, storage conditions, and lead times when planning orders. Collaboration with neighboring countries or global procurement mechanisms can help achieve viable order volumes for low-demand products. 13. Electronic Connectivity in Laboratories: Electronic communication systems can improve the efficiency of laboratory result delivery, particularly for early infant diagnosis. These systems have been successfully implemented in several countries and can be expanded to other diagnostic needs. 14. Equity and Feasibility: Electronic systems aim to improve access to diagnostic results in underserved areas, enhancing equity. Feasibility has been demonstrated in various settings, but considerations for data security and patient confidentiality are essential. 15. Research Gaps: Further studies are needed to assess the clinical impact of electronic result delivery systems on patient outcomes, including loss to follow-up, mortality, and morbidity.
